attributes.where: The Northwest Region and the surrounding grassland areas, with the West Region.
attributes.name: The Germans first used the term grassfields for the Bamenda highlands, which differ from the coastal forest.
attributes.peoples: Mainly the Tikar, Bamileke, Bamum, Ngemba, Widikum and Ngie groups, with Chamba-derived Bali chiefdoms.
attributes.centralised_fondoms: Kom (Bikom), Bafut, Nso and Bali are the main centralised fondoms the colonial authorities met.
attributes.tikar_share: In one study area the Tikar were about 60% of the population, represented by Nso', Oku, Mbum, Kom, Bafut, Yamba and Aghem.
attributes.terminology: A Fon rules a fondom, in the way a king rules a kingdom.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Fon (title) (CC BY-SA 4.0), and an anthropological paper on Northwest Grassfields chiefdoms. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.meaning: A chieftain or king of a region of Cameroon, especially among the Ngie, Widikum, Tikar and Bamileke peoples of the Bamenda Grassfields (Northwest and West regions) and in Lebialem in the Southwest Region.
attributes.local_words_for_king: Mfon in Mungaka, Ibyn in Kom, Ilon in Lamnso' and Ilo in Ngemba.
attributes.examples: Fons of Bafut, Nso, Bali Nyonga, Mankon, Oku, Bafanji and Fontem.
attributes.southwest_note: In the Southwest Region only Lebialem Division has Fons, the best known being the Fon of Fontem.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Bafut (CC BY-SA 4.0), Lonely Planet, and Moffor (2023), Technium Education and Humanities. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.location: About 20 km northwest of Bamenda, in Mezam Department, Northwest Region.
attributes.size: About 340 square kilometres, with 80,000 people in 2005, in 26 wards along 10 km of the Ring Road.
attributes.status: Traditionally the most powerful of the Grassfields kingdoms, whose Fons were paramount over many neighbours.
attributes.palace: The palace of the Fon of Bafut houses a museum.
attributes.festival: The annual festival Abin e Mfor (the dance of the Fon).
attributes.council: The Fon shared power with a council of elders called the Kwifor, restricted to commoners who had reached the rank of Bukum. It acted as kingmaker and a check on royal power.
attributes.german_period: In 1891 Bafut helped its neighbour Mankon, which was attacked by a German-led Bali Nyonga force. Relations with the Germans then worsened into the Bafut Wars of the early 20th century.
attributes.language: Bafut, a Mbam-Nkam language, and Cameroon Pidgin English.

source.citation: A University of Pretoria history of Bali Nyonga, and the Bum kingdom glossary of the Ethnographic Resource archive. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.origin: A Chamba Leko group that migrated from the Chamba area of northern Cameroon to the Bamenda Grassfields, mixing Western Grassfields, southern Bamum and Chamba elements.
attributes.palace: Galega I moved the palace to the present capital in about 1875.
attributes.german_period: An early ally of the German colonial forces, which strengthened its chiefs against other Grassfields chiefdoms.
attributes.name: Fonyonga means the Fon of the Nyonga people.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Bafut (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the Bum kingdom glossary. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.description: A council of elders in Grassfields kingdoms such as Bafut, whose members acted as kingmakers and a check on the Fon's power.
attributes.bafut_rule: Membership was restricted to commoners who had reached the rank of Bukum.
attributes.related_societies: In Nso a comparable regulatory society is the Ngwerong. Regulatory associations are called Kwi'fon in the Bum chiefdom.
